title: Unmold a tart from a loose-bottom pan: stand it on a cake stand and lower the ring away with both hands
instruction: Take the tart out of its pan.
context: A tart cannot be turned out upside down like a cake, because its crust and topping would break, so bakers (O*NET 51-3011.00) unmold it from a loose-bottom fluted pan another way. Lifted by its rim, the pan comes up whole, because the ring's inward bottom lip holds the loose base. Instead the baker holds the pan only by the outer rim, stands the base, centered, on something narrower than the base (America's Test Kitchen uses a can; here a small cake stand, so the tart ends ready to serve), and lowers the ring away level with both hands, so it drops to the counter and leaves the tart on its base, untouched. A ring lowered unevenly cocks, and its fluted wall levers into the baked crust edge and breaks it; a base set off center tips the tart off the stand.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A 24 cm (9.5-inch) fluted tart pan with a removable bottom, tinned steel, stands on the table centered at x 22.5, y 0: a ring whose wall is 2.6 cm tall with 30 flutes 2 mm deep, an inward bottom lip 1.25 cm wide (inner radius 10.6 cm, 4 mm thick) and a top rim; real pans have a 3 mm rolled rim, and here it is widened to a flat lip 1.2 cm wide (out to 26.7 cm across, 4 mm thick) so a gripper can pinch it; the ring weighs 150 g. The pan's loose base, a 23.4 cm steel disk 3 mm thick weighing 100 g, rests on the ring's bottom lip, and on it sits a baked tart 23.3 cm across and 2 cm tall with a fluted golden crust edge and a yellow filling, 450 g. A small plain white ceramic pedestal cake stand, 7 cm tall with an 11 cm top (narrower than the base and the ring's 21.2 cm bottom opening) on a 5 cm stem and a 9 cm foot, stands fixed on the table at x 41.5, y 0. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. It scores 0, irreversibly (2 control steps in a row), if a gripper's tool point or pad tip is ever over the tart's footprint (or 3 mm into its side) from the base's bottom (a tip that low is pinching the crust's edge) to 1 cm above its top, or if the tart ever tilts past 20 degrees or leaves its base (pushed more than 5 mm across it, which only a hand or the ring shoving its crust edge does, or lifted off it). It is 0 unless the base, with the tart on it, ends resting on the cake stand: its center within 3 cm of the stand's axis, within 5 degrees of level, its bottom within 5 mm of the stand's top, still. Then it is 0.25 if the ring is still on (the base on its bottom lip) or a tool point or pad tip is within 1 cm of the ring, base or tart; 0 if the ring is not flat on the table around the stand (its bottom within 5 mm of the table, within 5 degrees of level, the stand inside its 21.2 cm bottom opening); 0.5 if the ring ever tilted past 6 degrees while sliding down past the crust (its bottom 5 mm or more below where it holds the base and its top still above the base's bottom, a 1.7 cm stretch, judged over each step's travel with the ring tilted at both ends of the step; irreversible); 1.0 with both arms home (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started) and still, 0.9 with an arm not home. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. Why: 6 degrees leans the top of the 2.6 cm wall 2.7 mm inward, deeper than the 2 mm flutes, so the wall levers into the crust edge; within 3 cm of center the load stays well inside the stand's 5.5 cm top radius; 5 degrees drops the base's edge 1 cm. In a real trial, check on the video that no finger touched the tart, read the ring's tilt while lowering from a phone inclinometer taped to the lip, measure the base's offset on the stand with a ruler and photograph the fluted edge before and after.
reset_notes: Put the base back in the ring and a fresh baked tart shell (or the weighted card disk) on it, set the pan back at its spot and check the cake stand is at its spot.
fidelity: Full-size 24 cm pan; the cake stand is fixed; the tart is 450 g (a real filled one is 600 to 900 g) so two pinch grips on the lip carry it reliably. The rolled rim is widened to a 1.2 cm flat lip for the grippers. The ring's colliders are 24 straight segments, the wall's flutes are drawn but its collider is round, and the tart is one rigid body: crust breakage is scored from the ring's tilt and finger contact rather than simulated.
